content: The jaw refers to either of the two opposing structures located at or near the entrance to the mouth. These structures are responsible for opening and closing the mouth. The term jaws can also broadly describe the entire set of structures that form the roof of the mouth and facilitate its movement. In arthropods, the jaws are composed of chitin and move laterally. These structures may include mandibles, chelicerae, or, in some cases, pedipalps. Their primary functions are to acquire food, transport it to the mouth, and perform initial processing, such as mastication or chewing. In vertebrates, the jaws are typically made of bone or cartilage and move vertically. They consist of an upper jaw and a lower jaw. The lower jaw, also known as the mandible or dentary, is the mobile component. It articulates with the temporal bones of the skull at its posterior processes, called rami (singular: ramus). When the term jaw is used in the singular, it usually refers to the lower jaw. The upper jaw, or maxilla, is relatively fixed and is composed of two bones called the maxillae. These bones are fused at the midline by a suture. If this suture and surrounding structures fail to close properly during development, it can result in a condition known as cleft palate. The maxillae contribute to the formation of the roof of the mouth, the floor and sides of the nasal cavity, and the floor of the eye socket (orbit). The jaws typically house the teeth or serve as the foundation for the attachment of a beak. The evolution of the vertebrate jaw likely began during the Silurian period and first appeared in Placoderm fish, which further diversified during the Devonian period. It is believed that jaws evolved from the pharyngeal arches that support the gills in fish. Specifically, the two most anterior pharyngeal arches are thought to have developed into the jaw itself and the hyoid arch, which braces the jaw against the braincase, thereby improving mechanical efficiency. Although there is no direct fossil evidence to confirm this theory, it aligns with the observation that modern jawed vertebrates (Gnathostomes) possess seven pharyngeal arches, while primitive jawless vertebrates (Agnatha) have nine. Initially, the evolutionary advantage of the jaw may not have been related to feeding but rather to improved respiratory efficiency. Jaws were likely used in a buccal pump mechanism, which is still observable in modern fish and amphibians, to move water across the gills or air into the lungs. Over time, the role of jaws in feeding became more prominent and evolved into a critical function in vertebrates. In reptiles, the mandible is composed of five distinct bones. During the evolution of mammals, four of these bones were reduced in size and repurposed as part of the auditory system. These reduced bones are now known as the malleus and incus, which, along with the stapes (a more ancient structure), form the ossicles of the middle ear. This evolutionary adaptation offers several advantages. A single-bone jaw is structurally stronger, and the incorporation of the malleus and incus into the ear enhances hearing. However, reptiles, which often swallow their prey whole due to their slower digestive processes compared to mammals, may benefit from having multiple jaw bones. This configuration allows for greater flexibility, enabling the jaws to expand around large prey items.
